actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:

1. Exclude secondary causes: smoking/CO, obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea, living at altitude; drugs (testosterone, anabolic steroids, EPO). Check history for plethora, pruritus (especially after bath), splenomegaly.

2. If persistent unexplained or Hb >185 (male) / >165 (female): Check JAK2 V617F; serum EPO (low in polycythaemia vera). Refer Haematology for consideration of venesection and diagnostic workup. NICE CKS Polycythaemia.
3. Repeat: 4–6 weeks after addressing reversible causes; per Haematology if PV suspected.

triage: Assess: Chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, syncope, or severe dizziness?
Assess: Active GI bleed (melaena, haematemesis, large rectal bleed)?
Assess: New confusion or very pale/collapsed?
Disposition: Hb <70 g/L or any red flags → Urgent clinical assessment / A&E. Consider transfusion per local policy if symptomatic.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:

1. Use MCV to guide cause: Microcytic (iron deficiency – check ferritin, consider coeliac serology, FIT if appropriate); Normocytic (acute bleed, chronic disease, renal, haemolysis – check reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin); Macrocytic (B12/folate – check both; alcohol; hypothyroidism; MDS if persistent). NICE CKS Anaemia.

2. Iron deficiency: Treat cause (diet, bleeding). Oral iron (e.g. ferrous sulfate 200 mg OD or alternate day); recheck Hb and ferritin in 2–4 weeks. Consider IV iron if oral not tolerated or severe. If men or non-menstruating women, investigate GI tract (FIT, OGD/colonoscopy per 2WW if indicated).
3. B12/folate deficiency: Replace as per protocol; check intrinsic factor antibodies if B12 low (pernicious anaemia).
4. Unexplained or age ≥60 with iron deficiency: FIT and 2WW referral if positive or high risk. NICE NG12.
5. Repeat: Hb in 2–4 weeks after starting replacement; ferritin when repleting iron (aim normal then maintenance).
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Ensure no symptoms of anaemia (fatigue, SOB, pallor) or bleeding. If borderline (e.g. female 115–120), consider checking ferritin if symptomatic.
2. No active management if clinically well. Continue monitoring if on iron/B12 or chronic disease.
3. Repeat: Annual if monitoring (CKD, heart failure, previous deficiency); otherwise as clinically indicated.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

1. Microcytic anaemia: Iron deficiency most common – check ferritin, serum iron, TIBC/transferrin saturation. If iron replete, consider thalassaemia trait (Hb electrophoresis), chronic disease, or sideroblastic anaemia.
2. If iron deficient: Treat and investigate cause. In men and non-menstruating women, consider GI investigation (FIT, 2WW if indicated). Coeliac serology if dietary intake adequate. NICE CKS Anaemia.
3. Repeat: With Hb and ferritin in 2–4 weeks after starting iron.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

1. Macrocytosis: Check B12 and folate. Causes include B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, liver disease, drugs (methotrexate, azathioprine, phenytoin), pregnancy, MDS. If B12/folate normal and persistent, check TFTs; consider Haematology if unexplained. NICE CKS.
2. If B12/folate low: Replace and recheck FBC. If B12 low, consider intrinsic factor antibodies (pernicious anaemia).
3. Repeat: FBC in 2–4 weeks after replacement; MCV may take months to normalise.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Normocytic: Interpret with Hb. If anaemic, consider acute bleed, chronic disease, renal, early deficiency, or haemolysis (check reticulocytes).
2. Repeat: With FBC as indicated.

triage: Assess: Non-blanching rash, mottled/ashen skin, or cold extremities?
Assess: New confusion, lethargy, slurred speech, or reduced consciousness?
Assess: Rigors, severe myalgia, or anuria?
Disposition: If sepsis red flags or acutely unwell → Emergency admission (Sepsis 6).
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:

1. Check differential: Neutrophilia – infection, inflammation, steroids, smoking, myeloproliferative disorder. Lymphocytosis – viral (EBV, CMV), pertussis, CLL (if persistent, smear, refer). Eosinophilia – allergy, parasites, drugs, EGPA. NICE CKS.
2. If acute infection: Treat and recheck in 1–2 weeks. If persistent unexplained neutrophilia >15 or lymphocytosis >5 with lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly, consider Haematology referral and blood film.
3. Repeat: 1–2 weeks after infection resolved; sooner if concerning features.

triage: Assess: Fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, or signs of infection?
Assess: On chemotherapy, methotrexate, clozapine, or other myelosuppressive drug?
Disposition: WBC <1.0 or febrile neutropenia → Urgent A&E. WBC <2.0 or symptomatic → Urgent same-day assessment.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Causes: Drugs (MTX, azathioprine, carbimazole, clozapine, chemotherapy, sulfasalazine), viral infection, autoimmune, bone marrow failure, hypersplenism. Check drug history and recent infections.
2. If drug-related: Consider withholding if appropriate (per drug protocol); discuss with specialist. Clozapine: follow monitoring protocol. MTX: check folate; reduce or hold per Rheumatology.
3. If unexplained or persistent: FBC repeat in 1–2 weeks; blood film; consider viral serology (EBV, HIV if risk). Refer Haematology if WBC <1.5 or progressive. NICE CKS Neutropenia.
4. Repeat: 24–48 h if <2.0; 1–2 weeks if mild and stable.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Normal range. Interpret with clinical context and differential if requested.
2. Repeat: Routine or with FBC.

triage: Assess: Active bleeding, widespread purpura, or mucosal bleed?
Assess: New headache or neurological symptoms (possible intracranial bleed)?
Disposition: Platelets <20 or significant bleeding → Urgent Haematology / A&E.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Exclude pseudothrombocytopenia: EDTA-induced clumping – repeat in citrate tube if unexpected low count or no bleeding history.
2. Causes: Drugs (heparin, GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors, quinine, sulfonamides, valproate), viral infection, ITP, DIC, bone marrow failure, hypersplenism. Check medications and recent illness.
3. If 50–150 and no bleeding: Repeat in 1–2 weeks. If <50 or bleeding: Urgent Haematology. If <100 persistent: refer for workup (blood film, consider ITP). NICE CKS Thrombocytopenia.
4. Repeat: 1 week if 100–150; 24–48 h if <100 or symptomatic.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Reactive thrombocytosis: Iron deficiency (check ferritin), infection, inflammation, post-splenectomy, bleeding. Treat cause; platelets usually normalise.
2. If persistent >600 and no reactive cause: Check JAK2 V617F; consider Haematology referral for possible essential thrombocythaemia. NICE CKS.
3. Repeat: 4–6 weeks after treating cause; per Haematology if ET suspected.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Normal range. No action if no bleeding or bruising.
2. Repeat: Routine or with FBC.

triage: Assess: Is there new confusion, seizures, or decreased consciousness?
Assess: Is there severe headache, nausea, or vomiting?
Disposition: If any Red Flags present or Na < 125 mmol/L → Immediate Emergency Admission.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Fluid Status: Assess if Hypo/Eu/Hypervolaemic.
2. Meds Review: Check Diuretics, SSRIs, PPIs (Consider SIADH).
3. Malignancy: Screen for underlying causes if SIADH suspected.
4. Repeat: Within 48h if 130-132; Urgent Review/Repeat today if <130.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Review for symptoms of polydipsia if borderline low.
2. Action: No action required.
3. Repeat: Routine monitoring as indicated by comorbidities.

triage: Assess: Is the patient experiencing chest pain or palpitations?
Assess: Is there any new muscle weakness or paralysis?
Disposition: If any Red Flags present or K >= 6.5 mmol/L → Immediate Emergency Admission.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. URGENT: If K >= 6.0, obtain ECG immediately.
2. Sample Check: Review collection vs reporting time (Rule out Pseudohyperkalaemia).
3. Meds Review: Stop/Review ACEi, ARBs, Spironolactone, NSAIDs.
4. Repeat: Within 24-48h if 6.0-6.4; Urgent Repeat today if ≥6.5.

triage: Assess: Is there severe muscle weakness or palpitations?
Assess: Is the patient on Digoxin? (Increased toxicity risk).
Disposition: If K < 2.5 mmol/L or symptomatic → Immediate Emergency Admission.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Meds Check: Rule out Diuretics, Laxatives, or Insulin use.
2. Magnesium Check: Measure Magnesium (low Mg prevents K+ correction).
3. Supplementation: If 2.5-3.4 and asymptomatic, consider oral supplementation (Sando-K) or dietary increase.
4. Repeat: Recheck in 2-3 days if 3.0-3.4; Repeat today if 2.5-2.9.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Ensure patient is not on high-dose supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics.
2. Action: Continue current management.
3. Repeat: As per routine monitoring (6-12 months for ACEi/Diuretics).

triage: Assess: Is there significantly decreased urine output (<0.5ml/kg/hr)?
Assess: Is the patient vomiting or unable to tolerate oral fluids?
Disposition: If AKI Stage 3 or acutely unwell → Urgent Hospital Admission.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Meds Review: URGENTLY stop NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, Diuretics (Sick Day Rules).
2. Examination: Assess fluid status (Dehydration?) and bladder (Obstruction?).
3. Calculations: Check eGFR and compare to baseline (AKI criteria).
4. Repeat: Within 24-48h to monitor trend/resolution.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Ensure monitoring is up to date if patient has CKD or on high-risk meds.
2. Action: No action required.
3. Repeat: Routine monitoring as per local CKD/Medication policy.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Assess for dehydration or high-protein diet.
2. Action: Review together with Creatinine. If isolated high urea, consider GI bleed (upper).
3. Repeat: Routine or short interval if AKI suspected.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Action: Normal range.
2. Repeat: Routine.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Action: Normal range.
2. Repeat: Routine.

2. Action: If >3x ULN, check Viral Hepatitis Screen (HBsAg, HCV Ab). If persistent, request Liver US.

2. Action: If GGT high: biliary cause (US Liver). If GGT normal: Bone cause (Vit D/Calcium).
3. Repeat: Recheck in 4 weeks.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

2. Repeat: Routine.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Assess if conjugated or unconjugated. Rule out Gilbert's syndrome (common cause of isolated high bilirubin).
2. Action: If ALT/ALP also high, request Liver US. If jaundiced, urgent referral.
3. Repeat: Recheck in 2-4 weeks.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Action: Normal range.
2. Repeat: Routine.

2. Referral: Refer to Hepatology or Infectious Diseases for evaluation and viral load testing.
3. Repeat: Confirm with HCV RNA for Hep C.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Action: Screening negative.
2. Repeat: Only if new exposure/risk.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Action: All components within normal range.
2. Repeat: Routine annual screen if on medication monitoring.

triage: Assess: Severe lethargy, cold intolerance, bradycardia, or myxoedema (e.g. coarse skin, delayed reflexes)?
Assess: TSH >50 with very low Free T4 or confusion?
Disposition: If myxoedema or severe biochemical hypothyroidism with symptoms → Urgent Endocrinology / same-day assessment.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:

1. Request Free T4 to confirm primary hypothyroidism (high TSH + low Free T4). If Free T4 low: start levothyroxine. Dose 25–50 mcg OD (25 mcg if elderly, known IHD, or at risk); increase by 25 mcg every 4–6 weeks until TSH in target. NICE CKS Hypothyroidism.

2. Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4.5–10, Free T4 normal): Check TPO antibodies. Consider trial of levothyroxine if symptomatic or TPO positive; target TSH 0.4–2.0. If TSH >10 with normal Free T4, many guidelines suggest treat. NICE NG145.
3. Pregnancy: Use trimester-specific TSH (e.g. first trimester <2.5). Treat if TSH above pregnancy range; refer Obstetrics/Endocrinology. Do not use trimester-specific ranges for non-pregnant adults.
4. Repeat: TFTs 6–8 weeks after starting or changing levothyroxine. Once stable, annual TFTs.

triage: Assess: Palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance, weight loss, agitation, or atrial fibrillation?
Assess: Thyroid storm (fever, tachycardia, confusion, vomiting)?
Disposition: If thyroid storm or severe thyrotoxicosis → Emergency admission.
actions: MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Request Free T4 and Free T3. Suppressed TSH + raised Free T4 and/or Free T3 = primary hyperthyroidism. Refer Endocrinology for treatment (antithyroid drugs, radioiodine, or surgery). NICE NG145.
2. If on levothyroxine: Likely over-replacement. Reduce dose by 25 mcg; recheck in 6–8 weeks. Target TSH 0.4–2.0 (some prefer 0.5–2.5) in most adults.
3. Non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid): TSH can be low in acute illness; avoid starting treatment on a single result. Recheck when well.
4. Repeat: 4–6 weeks after dose change or per Endocrinology.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Euthyroid (TSH 0.4–4.5). If on levothyroxine, dose is adequate; continue. If symptomatic despite normal TSH, consider other causes (anaemia, mood, sleep).
2. Repeat: Annual TFTs if on thyroid treatment; otherwise as clinically indicated.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. With suppressed TSH: Confirms primary hyperthyroidism (Graves, toxic nodule, thyroiditis). Refer Endocrinology. Do not start levothyroxine. NICE NG145.
2. If on levothyroxine: Reduce dose by 25 mcg; recheck TSH and Free T4 in 6–8 weeks. Aim Free T4 in upper half of range only if TSH remains suppressed (e.g. pituitary disease) per specialist.
3. Pregnancy: Trimester-specific ranges apply; interpret with TSH. Refer if thyrotoxic.
4. Repeat: 4–6 weeks after dose change or per specialist.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. With raised TSH: Primary hypothyroidism. Start or increase levothyroxine (25–50 mcg OD; titrate by 25 mcg every 4–6 weeks). Recheck TFTs in 6–8 weeks. NICE CKS Hypothyroidism.
2. With low/normal TSH: Consider pituitary disease (secondary hypothyroidism) – refer Endocrinology; do not start levothyroxine without specialist advice if TSH inappropriately low.
3. Non-thyroidal illness: Low Free T4 with low/normal TSH can occur in severe illness; repeat when clinically recovered.
4. Repeat: 6–8 weeks after starting or increasing levothyroxine.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Normal range. Interpret with TSH: euthyroid if TSH normal; over-replaced if TSH suppressed.
2. Repeat: With TSH as per monitoring schedule.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. With suppressed TSH: Suggests T3-toxicosis (Free T4 may be normal) or hyperthyroidism. Refer Endocrinology. NICE NG145.
2. On levothyroxine: Usually not measured routinely; if high with suppressed TSH, reduce levothyroxine and recheck TSH/Free T4.
3. Repeat: Per Endocrinology or 4–6 weeks after treatment change.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

1. Often seen in non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid): Low T3 with low/normal TSH in acute illness, starvation, chronic disease. Do not treat with thyroid hormone; treat underlying condition. Recheck when well.
2. If hypothyroid (high TSH, low Free T4): Free T3 may be low; treat with levothyroxine (T3 is not routinely used in primary care for initiation).
3. Repeat: When clinically recovered if sick euthyroid; with TFTs if hypothyroid.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Normal range. Free T3 is less reliable than TSH/Free T4 for monitoring hypothyroidism; use mainly when hyperthyroidism or T3-toxicosis suspected.
2. Repeat: As per TSH/Free T4 indication.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Context: Infection (bacterial > viral), inflammation, flare of inflammatory arthritis (RA, seronegative), vasculitis.
2. Checks: Clinical picture – infection vs chronic disease. If arthritis: joint swelling, duration; consider RF and Anti-CCP if inflammatory arthritis suspected.
3. Action: Treat infection if indicated. If persistent unexplained >50–100, consider Rheumatology or other specialist review.
4. Repeat: After treatment or in 1–2 weeks if monitoring flare.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Confirm no clinical signs of acute infection or chronic inflammation.
2. Action: Reassure patient. Normal CRP suggests no significant active inflammation.
3. Repeat: Only if symptoms persist or new clinical concern arises.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Context: Infection, inflammatory arthritis (RA, PMR), GCA (if >50 and aged >50 with headache/jaw claudication – urgent), malignancy, anaemia (false elevation).
2. Checks: If aged >50 with shoulder/hip stiffness or headache – consider PMR/GCA; urgent if GCA suspected (prednisolone, same-day specialist).
3. Arthritis: Interpret with CRP, RF, Anti-CCP. Refer Rheumatology if inflammatory arthritis.
4. Repeat: After treatment or 4–6 weeks if monitoring.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Ensure no symptoms of PMR/GCA if aged >50.
2. Action: Normal ESR reduces likelihood of systemic inflammatory condition.
3. Repeat: Routine as indicated.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

2. Action: Start Loading doses of Hydroxocobalamin (6 injections over 2 weeks) then 3-monthly.
3. Repeat: Check FBC in 2-4 weeks to observe reticulocyte response.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

3. Repeat: Annual if on history of deficiency, otherwise routine.

3. Repeat: Recheck in 4 months.

2. Repeat: Routine.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Review for GI loss, menorrhagia, diet. If microcytic anaemia or strong suspicion, check coeliac serology (IgA tTG) and consider endoscopy if refractory.

2. Action: Confirm iron deficiency (low ferritin + low/normal transferrin sat). Start oral iron (e.g. ferrous sulfate 200 mg OD or bd); advise empty stomach, vitamin C. If intolerant, try alternate formulation or lower dose.
3. Referral: If symptomatic anaemia (Hb low), refractory to oral iron, or red flags (e.g. GI symptoms, >60) – consider 2WW and/or gastroenterology.
4. Repeat: Recheck Hb and ferritin in 2–4 weeks; continue until replete then 3 months to replenish stores.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Check CRP – normal CRP + ferritin >1000 suggests possible haemochromatosis; check Transferrin Saturation (>45–50% supports). Acute phase can raise ferritin.
2. Action: If CRP normal and ferritin persistently >1000, request HFE genetics if clinical suspicion (family history, arthropathy, diabetes, skin pigmentation).
3. Other causes: Fatty liver, metabolic syndrome, alcohol, inflammatory conditions.
4. Repeat: Re-test with CRP in 4–6 weeks if acute illness; if persistently raised, consider specialist review.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Checks: Ensure no signs of iron overload if high-normal (family history, joint pain).
2. Action: No action needed.
3. Repeat: Routine.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

2. Action: If iron deficiency confirmed, treat with oral iron and address cause (diet, bleeding, malabsorption).
3. Repeat: With ferritin in 2–4 weeks.
MANAGEMENT PLAN:

2. If Transferrin Saturation >45–50% and raised ferritin, consider HFE testing (haemochromatosis).

3. Repeat: Per specialist.

1. <10 mIU/mL: Non-responder after primary course. Complete second full course (0, 1, 6 months); check Anti-HBs 4–8 weeks after. If still <10 after 2 courses, check HBsAg (exclude chronic infection) and consider further doses or accept non-responder status. Document and advise re exposure risk. Green Book Ch 18.

2. 10–100 mIU/mL: Weak responder. Give one booster dose; re-check at 4–8 weeks. If >100 after booster, consider annual check for high-risk (e.g. dialysis, healthcare workers with exposure). PHE Green Book.

3. High-risk groups (healthcare, dialysis, household contacts of chronic HBV): Ensure immune; booster if waning. Repeat: 1–2 months after booster; then per occupational/renal policy (e.g. annual for dialysis).

1. Pre-diabetes (42–47 mmol/mol): Offer referral to National Diabetes Prevention Programme (NDPP). Lifestyle: weight loss, activity, diet. Re-test annually (or 6-monthly if high risk). NICE NG38, NG28.

Consider GLP-1 RA if BMI ≥35 and weight loss would help (NICE TA864). Review insulin if T2DM not at target on oral therapy.

4. HbA1c unreliable: Consider in anaemia, haemoglobinopathy, pregnancy, acute illness, haemolysis, RF – use fasting glucose or OGTT. In CKD (eGFR <60), HbA1c may be less accurate; use with clinical picture.
